name: Feedback
headline: Effective teachers use two-way feedback to gather information about student understanding, to help students advance their own learning, and to verify the impact of their own practice.
inContext: Two things make science feedback fail in predictable ways. First, timing: on an extended investigation, feedback that arrives with the mark arrives too late to be acted on, so it is read as a verdict rather than a direction. Second, volume — heavily annotated drafts produce compliance, not learning. The sustained fix is to design the feedback points into the task before the task is issued, each with a declared focus, no marks attached at the early points, and a requirement that students show what they did with the previous round. A depth study is the natural home for this because NESA already requires the extended timeframe.

context.label: Stage 6 Biology (2017) · Depth study — 15 hours of course time

exemplar.problem: Detailed written feedback on depth study drafts was almost entirely ignored. Students looked at the mark and filed the work. Feedback arrived at points where nothing could be changed, and the teacher was spending roughly six hours per class producing it.

phases.label: Design the feedback before the task
phases.what: Three feedback points are built into the task timeline, each with a declared and narrow focus.
phases.detail: Week 3 — research question and variables. Week 6 — method and data quality. Week 9 — analysis and evaluation. Students receive this schedule with the task notification, so they know exactly when feedback arrives and on what. Narrowing the focus is what makes the volume manageable: the teacher is not marking everything three times, but one thing well at the point it can still change.

phases.label: Feed forward, no marks
phases.what: The first round is task-focused, actionable, and deliberately carries no grade.
phases.detail: 'Your dependent variable can't be measured with the equipment you've listed' rather than 'good start' or a mark out of ten. The evidence is consistent that feedback about the task outperforms feedback about the person, and that attaching a grade suppresses engagement with the comment. Every comment ends with a next action, because feedback without a next action is a judgement.

phases.label: Self-assessment first, then conference
phases.what: Students bring their own judgement to a structured conference; the conversation is about the gap.
phases.detail: Peer feedback using a protocol students have been taught precedes a short student–teacher conference. The student self-assesses before the teacher speaks, and the discussion focuses on where the two judgements differ. This is what turns feedback into calibration — students learn to judge their own work accurately, which is the capability that outlives the task.

phases.label: Show what you did with it
phases.what: A short response-to-feedback log is submitted with the draft, and non-uptake is treated as a design problem.
phases.detail: Students record what each earlier comment asked, what they changed, and what they chose not to change and why — the last one matters, because a reasoned rejection is a legitimate scientific response. Where feedback was not taken up, the teacher's first question is whether it was actionable, not whether the student was diligent.

phases.label: Feedback in the other direction
phases.what: Students report which of the three points helped most, and that reshapes the schedule for the next cohort.
phases.detail: The HITS document is explicit that feedback is two-way and that teachers learn how their practice influences student learning. In the exemplar the Week 6 method conference was rated far more useful than the Week 9 analysis round, which led the faculty to move the third point earlier the following year.

exemplar.impact: Two measures that cost almost nothing. The proportion of Week 3 feedback points visibly actioned by Week 6, read directly off the drafts — a blunt but honest measure of whether feedback is landing. And the size of the gap between student self-assessment and teacher assessment across the three points, which should narrow if calibration is developing.

transfer.label: Stage 4–5 · practical reports
transfer.text: The same architecture, compressed. Feedback on one section only per practical report across a unit — aim and hypothesis in the first, method in the second, conclusion in the third — so students receive less feedback per report but can act on all of it, and the teacher's marking load falls rather than rises.

teacher: Schedules feedback points into the task timeline before the task is issued
Gives early feedback without marks attached, focused on the task and not the person
Ends every comment with an action the student can actually take
Requires students to self-assess before receiving teacher feedback
Treats feedback that wasn't acted on as a problem with the feedback
notDemonstrated: Feedback is about the person ('you're one of my strongest students') or vague ('good work')
Feedback only arrives with the summative mark, when nothing can change
Extensive annotation is produced that students have no opportunity to use
Students are never asked to judge their own work before being told
Student feedback on teaching is never sought
student: Understand specifically what they need to do to improve
Can point to what they changed in response to earlier feedback
Judge their own work against the criteria before submitting
Use feedback to monitor and self-regulate, not merely to comply

continuum.label: Emerging
continuum.text: Teachers provide students with feedback on strengths and areas for improvement.

continuum.label: Evolving
continuum.text: Feedback is targeted, based on informed and timely judgements of each student's achievement relative to their goals and needs.

continuum.label: Embedding
continuum.text: Formative and summative strategies are used across the faculty with timely feedback supporting individualised learning, and assessment data feeds back into teaching practice.

continuum.label: Excelling
continuum.text: Comprehensive assessment data underpins regular feedback to students and parents. Teachers analyse data to reflect on practice, and student feedback actively informs teaching.

evidence: Hattie (2009): feedback 0.73; Evidence for Learning: +8 months. Hattie and Timperley (2007) on feedback about the task outperforming praise, punishment and rewards; Kluger and DeNisi (1996) on task-focused feedback. Effective feedback is one of the eight CESE What Works Best themes. NESA Stage 6 syllabuses allocate 15 hours of course time to depth studies in each of Year 11 and Year 12.
